# GPU-NTT

Welcome to the GPU-NTT-Optimization repository! We present cutting-edge algorithms and implementations for optimizing the Merge and 4-Step Number Theoretic Transforms (NTT) on GPUs. GPU-NTT automatically supports both 32-bit and 64-bit arithmetic via Barrett reduction; the older manual reduction selection is kept in the paper_version branch.

The associated research paper: https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/1410

FFT variant of GPU-NTT is available: https://github.com/Alisah-Ozcan/GPU-FFT

## Development

### Requirements

  * CMake >=3.26
  * GCC
  * CUDA Toolkit

### Build & Install

Configure + build:
    
    cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86
    cmake --build build --parallel

Install:
    
    cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86
    cmake --build build --parallel
    cmake --install build

Notes:

  * If you install to a system location (default: `/usr/local`), you may need `sudo` or set `-DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=/your/prefix`.
  * If you omit `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=...`, GPU-NTT defaults to `80;86;89;90`.
  * If CMake cannot find `nvcc`, set `CUDACXX=/path/to/nvcc` or pass `-DCMAKE_CUDA_COMPILER=/path/to/nvcc`.
  * If you change compilers/toolchains, prefer a clean configure: `cmake --fresh -S . -B build`.

### Compile Options

GPU-NTT uses C++17/CUDA17 and applies per-configuration compile flags.

  * Build type (single-config generators like Makefiles/Ninja): `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release|Debug|RelWithDebInfo|MinSizeRel`
  * Optimization/debug defaults:
    * `Release`: `-O3 -DNDEBUG`
    * `RelWithDebInfo`: `-O3 -g -DNDEBUG`
    * `Debug`: `-g` (and CUDA adds line info)
  * Extra warnings: `-DGPUNTT_ENABLE_WARNINGS=ON`

Example:
    
    cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo -DGPUNTT_ENABLE_WARNINGS=ON

## Using GPU-NTT in a downstream CMake project

Make sure GPU-NTT is installed before integrating it into your project. The installed GPU-NTT library provides a set of config files that make it easy to integrate GPU-NTT into your own CMake project. In your CMakeLists.txt, simply add:
    
    project(<your-project> LANGUAGES CXX CUDA)
    find_package(CUDAToolkit REQUIRED)
    # ...
    find_package(GPUNTT CONFIG REQUIRED)
    # ...
    target_link_libraries(<your-target> (PRIVATE|PUBLIC|INTERFACE) GPUNTT::ntt CUDA::cudart)
    # ...
    set_target_properties(<your-target> PROPERTIES CUDA_SEPARABLE_COMPILATION ON)
    # ...

Chimera: A Hybrid GPU Backend for Sumcheck Acceleration in Zero-Knowledge Provers

Kashfia Farheen and Nektarios Georgios Tsoutsos

Show abstract

Implementation

Sumcheck is increasingly used in proof systems based on multilinear polynomials, but its execution structure differs from that of conventional GPU targets such as MSM and NTT. Each round contains substantial data-parallel polynomial computation, but consecutive rounds depend on challenges derived from previous rounds and interact with the surrounding prover's proof-generation operations. Efficient acceleration therefore depends not only on GPU arithmetic throughput, but also on where polynomial data resides, what crosses the CPU-GPU boundary, and when execution should return to the CPU. We present Chimera, a hybrid CPU-GPU backend for Sumcheck computations in the Spartan R1CS prover. Chimera keeps large polynomial data on the GPU across profitable rounds, returns only the compact polynomial values needed by Spartan's transcript, and sends the resulting challenge back to the GPU for folding. It switches sufficiently small late rounds to Spartan's native CPU implementation. When polynomial data exceeds GPU memory, Chimera processes it in smaller portions and transitions to resident GPU execution once the remaining data fits. Chimera preserves Spartan's proof format and verifier behavior while also reducing CPU-side overhead directly surrounding the accelerated Sumcheck computations. On BN254 Spartan R1CS instances, Chimera reduces the measured Sumcheck-related region from \(672.785\) ms to \(84.245\) ms at \(N=2^{17}\), a \(7.99\times\) speedup. Complete proving time improves at every measured size, reaching \(1.27\times\)-\(1.64\times\) speedup for \(N=2^{24}\)-\(2^{27}\). Separately, our standalone quadratic GPU Sumcheck executes in \(28.7\) ms at \(N=2^{22}\), compared with \(84.2\) ms for ICICLE's CUDA Sumcheck implementation, a \(2.94\times\) GPU-to-GPU improvement. These results show that effective Sumcheck acceleration depends on both efficient GPU execution and careful integration with the surrounding proof system.

Speeding up Sumcheck using Algebraic Geometry

Rahul Dalal, Benedikt Bunz, Tamir Hemo, and Ron D. Rothblum

Show abstract

Cryptographic protocols

The sumcheck protocol, a ubiquitous component of modern proof-systems, enables proving the sum of evaluations of a low-degree multivariate polynomial. In theory, sumcheck has been generalized from polynomials to (tensors of) any multiplication code, a code whose pointwise products of codewords lie in a related product code. All practical systems nonetheless specifically use polynomials. For proof-systems over binary fields that target Boolean circuits, this choice has a real cost: the product of two binary messages under Reed--Solomon is no longer binary. As a result, the prover's work in the first, and most expensive, round of sumcheck (the so-called univariate skip) grows by a logarithmic factor. We present a new concrete multiplication code based on algebraic geometry that is binary-preserving: the product of two encoded binary messages is again a binary message. Specifically, we construct an explicit multiplication code over $\mathbb{F}_{2^{128}}$ that carries $64$-bit messages to binary product messages of length $222$, and whose product code has relative distance greater than $1-2^{-119}$. The part of the product message that the prover actually sends in sumcheck is more than $3 \times$ smaller than with Reed--Solomon, as used in practice. The code comes from a genus-$95$ curve over $\mathbb{F}_2$ with $64$ rational points, built as a $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^3$ Artin--Schreier cover of a genus-$4$ curve. We implemented the resulting protocol, which we call the AG skip, inside the Flock proof-system. For $2^{32}$ constraints, it speeds up the skip round by $2.36\times$ and the whole zerocheck, which was the prover's most expensive component, by $1.65\times$.
We further consider two variants: an XFL-based method that combines partial Gaussian elimination with variable guessing, and a WXL-based method that exploits the sparsity of the Macaulay matrix. Our complexity analysis for various parameter settings shows that, for some fixed values of $n$ and $k$, the WXL-based variant using a larger solving degree $d>2$ is particularly efficient when the block size $\beta$ is sufficiently small, while the original hybrid algorithm becomes more efficient as $\beta$ increases.

4.3 SEAL CKKS GPU Implementation

In this section, we present the GPU implementation of the CKKS homomorphic operation algorithms, which include homomorphic addition, homomorphic multiplication, rescaling, relinearization, and rotation. To develop these algorithms, we utilize the Microsoft SEAL library. Initially, we created Python models and pseudocode to outline the implementation process on the GPU. Subsequently, we commenced the GPU implementation.

4.3.1 Homomorphic Addition

Homomorphic addition is one of the simplest and least expensive operations in the CKKS scheme. As depicted in Algorithm 5, it involves only element-wise addition operations. Therefore, the implementation consists of only one kernel with a maximum thread count allowed by the GPU, which is 1024 threads for each block. The kernel has 2 × decomposition_mod_count × (r/thread_num) blocks, where decomposition_mod_count = r − 1 and r = number of RNS bases.

L23: 
L24: This tutorial walks you through building a batched staged Number Theoretic Transform round-trip at N=16384 using cuPQC-NTT. You'll learn how `SubSize<M>` decomposes one large transform into two kernel passes, how to write the stage kernels for both directions, and how to size the shared memory and launch geometry each pass needs.
L25: The NTT is the modular-arithmetic analogue of the FFT: it turns polynomial multiplication into cheap pointwise multiplication, which is why it sits on the critical path of lattice-based post-quantum schemes, fully homomorphic encryption, and zero-knowledge proof systems. A single-pass transform keeps its entire workspace in one block's shared memory, so it stops scaling once N grows past what a block can hold.
L26: The staged API solves exactly that problem: with `SubSize<M>` and `K = N / M`, each pass bounds its per-block working set to `max(K, M)` elements rather than the full N, so the transform no longer has to fit in a single block at all.
L27: cuPQC-NTT requires cuPQC SDK 0.6.0 or newer, the release that introduced it. cuPQC 0.6 targets compute capabilities 8.0, 8.6, 8.7, 8.9, and 9.0. The library implements the cyclic transform, meaning arithmetic in the ring modulo x^{N} - 1.
L28: ## Step 1: Project Setup
L29: 
L30: Clone the cuPQC repository:
L31: 
L32:     `git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuPQC.git
L33:     cd cuPQC/examples/ntt
L34:     `
L35: 
L36: This will download all examples including the staged NTT example. The Makefile in this directory will compile all examples, including `example_staged_ntt`.
L37: ## Step 2: Include Required Headers
L38: 
L39: Start by including the necessary cuPQC SDK headers:
L40: 
L41:     `#include <cstdlib>
L42:     #include <vector>
L43:     #include <iostream>
L44: 
L45:     #include <ntt.hpp>
L46: 
L47:     using namespace cupqc;
L48:     `
L49: 
L50: The `ntt.hpp` header provides the NTT descriptor operators, the staged transform entry points, the built-in prime fields, and the precomputed roots of unity.
L51: ## Step 3: Understand the Staged Decomposition
L52: 
L53: Choose N and the sub-size M up front, since both go into the descriptor as compile-time constants:
L54: 
L55:     `constexpr uint32_t NTT_N = 16384;
L56:     constexpr uint32_t NTT_M = 256;
L57:     constexpr uint32_t NTT_K = NTT_N / NTT_M;  // 64
L58:     `
L59: 
L60: `SubSize<M>` splits an N-point NTT into two successive kernel passes with `K = N / M`:
L61:   * Forward stage 1 runs `M` blocks, each performing a `K`-point transform over contiguous elements.
L62:   * Forward stage 2 runs `K` blocks, each performing an `M`-point transform over strided elements.
L63: The inverse reverses the stage ordering — its stage 1 is the `M`-point strided pass and its stage 2 is the `K`-point contiguous pass — and applies the `1/N` normalization in stage 2. Neither pass ever needs more than `max(K, M)` elements of shared memory, which for N=16384 with M=256 means 256 elements instead of 16384.
L64: Staged transforms cover `2^14` through `2^24` points, and the allowed `SubSize<M>` values narrow as N grows, so consult the feature documentation before committing to a pair. This example uses N = 16384 = 2^{14}, split as M = 256, K = 64.
L65: ## Step 4: Define the Staged NTT Types
L66: Define one descriptor per direction. The staged behavior comes entirely from adding `SubSize<M>()` to an otherwise ordinary block-execution NTT descriptor:
L67: 
L68:     `using ForwardNTT = decltype(Algorithm<algorithm::NTT>()
L69:                                 + Direction<nttDirection::FORWARD>()
L70:                                 + Precision<uint32_t>()
L71:                                 + Size<NTT_N>()
L72:                                 + SubSize<NTT_M>()
L73:                                 + Block()
L74:                                 + BlockDim<128>());
L75: 
L76:     using InverseNTT = decltype(Algorithm<algorithm::NTT>()
L77:                                 + Direction<nttDirection::INVERSE>()
L78:                                 + Precision<uint32_t>()
L79:                                 + Size<NTT_N>()
L80:                                 + SubSize<NTT_M>()
L81:                                 + Block()
L82:                                 + BlockDim<128>());
L83:     `
L84: `Algorithm<algorithm::NTT>()` selects the transform.
L85: `Direction<nttDirection::FORWARD>()` and `Direction<nttDirection::INVERSE>()` pick the direction; the two descriptors are otherwise identical.
L86: `Precision<uint32_t>()` selects the coefficient and modulus width. `uint16_t`, `uint32_t`, and `uint64_t` are supported.
L87: `Size<NTT_N>()` sets the transform length.
L88: `SubSize<NTT_M>()` requests the staged decomposition with sub-size M, which is what makes the stage entry points available.
L89: `Block()` with `BlockDim<128>()` requests block execution with 128 threads per block.
L90: The descriptors expose the constants used later on: `ForwardNTT::Size` is N and `ForwardNTT::BlockDim` is the thread count, so the launch code never has to repeat them.
L91: Both examples in this directory use KoalaBear, `p = 2^31 - 2^24 + 1`, which supports NTT sizes up to 2^{24}:
L92: 
L93:     `constexpr uint32_t p = cupqc::KoalaBear;                    // KoalaBear prime
L94:     constexpr uint32_t g = cupqc::KoalaBear_primitive_root_14;  // primitive 2^14-th root of unity mod p
L95: 
L96:     const uint32_t g_inv = host_modpow(g, p - 2, p);  // g^{-1} mod p
L97:     const uint32_t N_inv = 2130576385;                // (2^14)^{-1} mod p
L98:     `
L99: `KoalaBear_primitive_root_14` is one of the precomputed `*_primitive_root_S` constants for transform size 2^{S}. The inverse root is derived on the host with a small modular-exponentiation helper (`host_modpow`) using Fermat's little theorem, and `N_inv` is the `1/N` factor the inverse transform needs.
L100: ## Step 5: Generate the Twiddle Tables
L101: Twiddle generation is identical to the single-pass transform — the staged decomposition reuses the same tables across both of its passes:
L102: 
L103:     `template<class NTT>
L104:     __global__ void make_twiddles_kernel(uint32_t* twiddles, const uint32_t p, const uint32_t g) {
L105:         NTT().make_twiddles(twiddles, p, g);
L106:     }
L107: 
L108:     template<class NTT>
L109:     __global__ void transform_twiddles_to_mont_kernel(uint32_t* twiddles, const uint32_t p) {
L110:         NTT().transform_twiddles_to_mont(twiddles, p);
L111:     }
L112:     `
L113: Generate one table per direction and convert both into the Montgomery domain. This happens once and the tables are then reused for the entire batch:
L114: 
L115:     `const nttConst<uint32_t> scheme_const(p);
L116: 
L117:     make_twiddles_kernel<ForwardNTT><<<1, 1>>>(d_twiddles,     p, g);
L118:     make_twiddles_kernel<InverseNTT><<<1, 1>>>(d_inv_twiddles, p, g_inv);
L119:     transform_twiddles_to_mont_kernel<ForwardNTT><<<1, ForwardNTT::BlockDim>>>(d_twiddles, p);
L120:     transform_twiddles_to_mont_kernel<InverseNTT><<<1, InverseNTT::BlockDim>>>(d_inv_twiddles, p);
L121:     `
L122: The forward table is built from `g`, the inverse table from `g^-1 mod p`. `nttConst<uint32_t>` bundles the modulus and its derived Montgomery constants; it is constructed on the host from `p` and passed to the kernels by value.
L123: ## Step 6: Write the Forward Stage Kernels
L124: Each stage is its own kernel, and each follows the same load, execute, store pattern as the single-pass transform, with stage-qualified entry points. Both kernels take the polynomial base pointer and a `batch_id`, and use `extern __shared__` so the workspace size can be chosen per stage at launch time:
L125: 
L126:     `__global__ void fwd_stage_1_kernel(uint32_t* data, const uint32_t* twiddles,
L127:                                        const nttConst<uint32_t> scheme_const, const int batch_id) {
L128:         extern __shared__ uint32_t sdata[];
L129:         ForwardNTT().stage_1_load_to_mont(sdata, data + batch_id * ForwardNTT::Size, blockIdx.x, scheme_const);
L130:         __syncthreads();
L131:         ForwardNTT().stage_1_execute(sdata, twiddles, scheme_const.p);
L132:         __syncthreads();
L133:         ForwardNTT().stage_1_store(sdata, data + batch_id * ForwardNTT::Size, blockIdx.x);
L134:     }
L135: 
L136:     __global__ void fwd_stage_2_kernel(uint32_t* data, const uint32_t* twiddles,
L137:                                        const nttConst<uint32_t> scheme_const, const int batch_id) {
L138:         extern __shared__ uint32_t sdata[];
L139:         ForwardNTT().stage_2_load(sdata, data + batch_id * ForwardNTT::Size, blockIdx.x);
L140:         __syncthreads();
L141:         ForwardNTT().stage_2_execute(sdata, twiddles, scheme_const.p);
L142:         __syncthreads();
L143:         ForwardNTT().stage_2_store_from_mont(sdata, data + batch_id * ForwardNTT::Size, blockIdx.x, scheme_const);
L144:     }
L145:     `
L146: Device transforms operate on Montgomery-domain data, so conversion happens at the memory boundary rather than per operation. Notice where that boundary falls across the two passes: stage 1 converts on the way in with `stage_1_load_to_mont` but stores with plain `stage_1_store`, and stage 2 reads with plain `stage_2_load` and only converts back out with `stage_2_store_from_mont`.
L147: The intermediate result written to global memory between the passes therefore stays in the Montgomery domain, and the round trip through global memory costs no conversions.
L148: Every stage entry point takes `blockIdx.x` explicitly. That is how a block learns which sub-transform it owns, and it is what lets the same pointer serve `M` blocks in stage 1 and `K` blocks in stage 2. Both stages operate on the same polynomial pointer, and stage 2 reads the output that stage 1 wrote, so the kernel launch order is the dependency.
L149: ## Step 7: Write the Inverse Stage Kernels
L150: The inverse kernels mirror the forward ones, with one addition: `stage_2_execute` takes `N_inv` and applies the `1/N` normalization as part of the final pass.
L151: 
L152:     `__global__ void inv_stage_1_kernel(uint32_t* data, const uint32_t* inv_twiddles,
L153:                                        const nttConst<uint32_t> scheme_const, const int batch_id) {
L154:         extern __shared__ uint32_t sdata[];
L155:         InverseNTT().stage_1_load_to_mont(sdata, data + batch_id * InverseNTT::Size, blockIdx.x, scheme_const);
L156:         __syncthreads();
L157:         InverseNTT().stage_1_execute(sdata, inv_twiddles, scheme_const.p);
L158:         __syncthreads();
L159:         InverseNTT().stage_1_store(sdata, data + batch_id * InverseNTT::Size, blockIdx.x);
L160:     }
L161: 
L162:     __global__ void inv_stage_2_kernel(uint32_t* data, const uint32_t* inv_twiddles,
L163:                                        const nttConst<uint32_t> scheme_const, const uint32_t N_inv,
L164:                                        const int batch_id) {
L165:         extern __shared__ uint32_t sdata[];
L166:         InverseNTT().stage_2_load(sdata, data + batch_id * InverseNTT::Size, blockIdx.x);
L167:         __syncthreads();
L168:         InverseNTT().stage_2_execute(sdata, inv_twiddles, scheme_const.p, N_inv);
L169:         __syncthreads();
L170:         InverseNTT().stage_2_store_from_mont(sdata, data + batch_id * InverseNTT::Size, blockIdx.x, scheme_const);
L171:     }
L172:     `

L31: ### cite17†Chimera: A Hybrid GPU Backend for Sumcheck Acceleration in Zero-Knowledge Provers L32: 
L33: Kashfia Farheen, University of Delaware
L34: 
L35: Nektarios Georgios Tsoutsos, University of Delaware
L36: ##### Abstract
L37: Sumcheck is increasingly used in proof systems based on multilinear polynomials, but its execution structure differs from that of conventional GPU targets such as MSM and NTT. Each round contains substantial data-parallel polynomial computation, but consecutive rounds depend on challenges derived from previous rounds and interact with the surrounding prover's proof-generation operations.
L38: Efficient acceleration therefore depends not only on GPU arithmetic throughput, but also on where polynomial data resides, what crosses the CPU-GPU boundary, and when execution should return to the CPU. We present Chimera, a hybrid CPU-GPU backend for Sumcheck computations in the Spartan R1CS prover.
L39: Chimera keeps large polynomial data on the GPU across profitable rounds, returns only the compact polynomial values needed by Spartan's transcript, and sends the resulting challenge back to the GPU for folding. It switches sufficiently small late rounds to Spartan's native CPU implementation. When polynomial data exceeds GPU memory, Chimera processes it in smaller portions and transitions to resident GPU execution once the remaining data fits.
L40: Chimera preserves Spartan's proof format and verifier behavior while also reducing CPU-side overhead directly surrounding the accelerated Sumcheck computations. On BN254 Spartan R1CS instances, Chimera reduces the measured Sumcheck-related region from \(672.785\) ms to \(84.245\) ms at \(N=2^{17}\), a \(7.99\times\) speedup. Complete proving time improves at every measured size, reaching \(1.27\times\)-\(1.64\times\) speedup for \(N=2^{24}\)-\(2^{27}\).
L41: Separately, our standalone quadratic GPU Sumcheck executes in \(28.7\) ms at \(N=2^{22}\), compared with \(84.2\) ms for ICICLE's CUDA Sumcheck implementation, a \(2.94\times\) GPU-to-GPU improvement. These results show that effective Sumcheck acceleration depends on both efficient GPU execution and careful integration with the surrounding proof system.

L43: cite19†Attacks and cryptanalysis L44: Pseudorandom Generators (PRGs) based on Threshold-XOR predicates with large locality and high stretches have recently gained traction, since they lend themselves as shallow weak Pseudorandom Functions (PRFs) to fast multiparty computation protocols. In this work, we present novel fast attacks on such PRGs that achieve substantial advantages.
L45: Concretely, we break the security levels of most parameters collected by Boura, Couteau, Perrin and Rotella (ToSC'25), as well as those proposed by Fu, Li, Lyu and Liu (EC'26). As a consequence, when $a \in \Theta(n)$, we get poly-time attacks with noticeable advantage.
L46: These results close current gaps on the theoretical study of THR-XOR based Goldreich PRGs. Additionally, we demonstrate how the attack advantage can be amplified for PRGs with large output lengths (which are common in the context of weak PRFs). Finally, we discuss alternative predicates for Goldreich PRGs that resist all currently known attacks.

L221: # cuPQC SDK Applications
L222: 
L223: This repository contains examples demonstrating the capabilities of NVIDIA cuPQC SDK.
L224: 
L225: What's included:
L226: 
L227:   * Example applications with build configs
L228:   * Reference implementations
L229: ## About cuPQC SDK
L230: 
L231: NVIDIA cuPQC is a GPU-accelerated cryptography SDK containing specialized libraries for building high-performance cryptographic applications:
L232: 
L233:   * cuPQC-HASH - Hash functions & Merkle Trees
L234:   * cuPQC-PK - Public-Key Cryptography (ML-KEM & ML-DSA)
L235:   * cuPQC-BigInt - Multi-Precision Integer Arithmetic
L236:   * cuPQC-NTT - Number Theoretic Transforms
L237: ## Applications & Examples
L238: 
L239: Applications: Browse cite93†applications/ directory for application implementations.
L240: 
L241: Examples: Browse cite94†examples/ directory for examples demonstrating individual SDK primitives:
L242: 
L243:   * Hash Functions (SHA-2, SHA-3, Poseidon2, Merkle Trees)
L244:   * Multi-Precision Integers (wide addition, modular multiplication, pihex)
L245:   * Number Theoretic Transforms (standard and staged round-trips)
L246:   * Public-Key Cryptography (ML-KEM, ML-DSA)
L247:

These libraries are engineered to power the entire cryptographic spectrum, from classical protocols and post-quantum cryptography (PQC) to the massive computational workloads at the core of Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) and Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE). ## What's New in 0.6 Whether you are scaling traditional public-key cryptography like RSA and ECC, implementing post-quantum schemes, or bringing advanced privacy-preserving technologies like ZKPs and FHE to production, you face the same bottleneck: executing millions of multi-precision integer operations and polynomial multiplications at high throughput. Historically, accelerating these workloads on GPUs meant implementing and optimizing custom CUDA kernels from scratch for every specific ring dimension, bit width, and parameter set your schemes require. cuPQC 0.6 eliminates this barrier by providing that arithmetic through the cuPQC-BigInt and cuPQC-NTT libraries as ready-to-use GPU primitives. You can now compose complex cryptographic protocols using accelerated multi-precision integer arithmetic and polynomial multiplication as standard building blocks. These libraries are designed as device extensions, enabling you to fuse these arithmetic operations with your own specialized functions into a single kernel. This avoids unnecessary host-device data transfers and intermediate memory allocations, a critical requirement for applications like ZKP proving, FHE ciphertext evaluation, and large-scale public-key infrastructure. Batch-oriented APIs enable thousands of concurrent operations to execute in parallel, letting you build faster, more scalable cryptographic solutions while focusing on your protocol design rather than arithmetic implementation. L23: 
L24: August 28, 2026 cuPQC SDK v0.6
L25: We're excited to announce cuPQC 0.6, delivering Big Integer Arithmetic (BigInt) and the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) as foundational math layer primitives specifically built for cryptographic application developers working on NVIDIA GPUs. These libraries are engineered to power the entire cryptographic spectrum, from classical protocols and post-quantum cryptography (PQC) to the massive computational workloads at the core of Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) and Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE).
L26: ## What's New in 0.6
L27: Whether you are scaling traditional public-key cryptography like RSA and ECC, implementing post-quantum schemes, or bringing advanced privacy-preserving technologies like ZKPs and FHE to production, you face the same bottleneck: executing millions of multi-precision integer operations and polynomial multiplications at high throughput.
L28: Historically, accelerating these workloads on GPUs meant implementing and optimizing custom CUDA kernels from scratch for every specific ring dimension, bit width, and parameter set your schemes require.
L29: cuPQC 0.6 eliminates this barrier by providing that arithmetic through the cuPQC-BigInt and cuPQC-NTT libraries as ready-to-use GPU primitives. You can now compose complex cryptographic protocols using accelerated multi-precision integer arithmetic and polynomial multiplication as standard building blocks.
L30: These libraries are designed as device extensions, enabling you to fuse these arithmetic operations with your own specialized functions into a single kernel. This avoids unnecessary host-device data transfers and intermediate memory allocations, a critical requirement for applications like ZKP proving, FHE ciphertext evaluation, and large-scale public-key infrastructure.
L31: Batch-oriented APIs enable thousands of concurrent operations to execute in parallel, letting you build faster, more scalable cryptographic solutions while focusing on your protocol design rather than arithmetic implementation.
L32: This release adds:
L33:   * cuPQC-BigInt: Provides fixed-width unsigned integers with full arithmetic up to 4096 bits and storage up to 8192 bits, with thread and warp execution models, Barrett and Montgomery reduction paths, and compile-time error-handling policies. It serves as the workhorse for classical cryptography, the classical halves of hybrid PQC protocols, and large-field ZKP arithmetic.
L34:   * cuPQC-NTT: Provides cyclic forward and inverse transforms in the Montgomery domain, in both standard and staged execution modes, for transform lengths up to 2^{24} points over a user-selected prime up to 62 bits. This provides the exact heavy lifting required for the massive polynomial rings used in FHE and ZKP systems.
L35: In our benchmarks, cuPQC-NTT runs 32-bit transforms 12× to 42× faster than a 28-core CPU across sizes from 2^{8} to 2^{24} points, and cuPQC-BigInt runs 34× to 773× faster than a single CPU core running GMP across the eight operations we measured.
L36: These additions expand the cuPQC SDK into four libraries across two tiers. At the math layer, cuPQC-BigInt and cuPQC-NTT provide low-level arithmetic, while cuPQC-Hash delivers key ZKP primitives like Poseidon2 and Merkle trees. Together, they give developers full flexibility to either deploy ready-to-use algorithms or construct custom, high-performance cryptographic pipelines on GPUs.

The NTT is the modular-arithmetic analogue of the Fast Fourier Transform and is a core building block of lattice-based cryptography, zero-knowledge proof systems, and modular ring arithmetic over finite fields.
L56: As a device-side library, cuPQC-NTT integrates directly into your CUDA kernels, enabling you to fuse NTTs with other GPU computations for maximum performance. Transforms run in the Montgomery domain; convert at load/store boundaries and convert twiddle tables once before reuse.
L57: The notation in the panel below is used throughout the rest of this page for transform lengths and two-pass tiling.
L58: 
L59: Notation for `N`, `M`, `K`, and `d`
L60: 
L61: Transform length `N` is a power-of-two, with N =`2`^{`d`} and `d` = log_{2}(`N`).
L62: 
L63: Sub-transform size `M` (a power-of-two) is set with `SubSize<M>`; `K = N/M`.
L64: ## NTT Transform Modescite43†# L65: 
L66: The cuPQC-NTT library provides two execution modes:
L67: 
L68:   * Standard NTT: A complete `N`-point transform is performed in a single kernel launch per length-`N` buffer, with the full working set held in shared memory. This mode is ideal for transform lengths that fit within available shared memory.
L69:   * Staged NTT: For large `N`, per-block shared memory cannot hold the full workspace for an `N`-point transform in a single pass, so a staged NTT is required. With `SubSize<M>` and two kernel passes: the first stage runs `M` parallel `K`-point contiguous NTTs (`K = N/M`); the second runs `K` parallel `M`-point strided NTTs. Each stage limits the per-block working set to `max(K, M)` elements, enabling transforms that would not fit in a single block’s shared memory.
L70: ## Supported Configurationscite44†# L71: 
L72: The table below summarizes the supported Execution Modes, Transform Type, Prime Fields, and Precomputed Roots.
L73: Aspect  | Summary
L74: --- | ---
L75: Execution modes  | Standard: One-kernel transform of length-`N`. Staged: Two-kernel transforms of `(N, SubSize<M>)` pairs.
L76: Transform type  | Cyclic: Length-`N` transforms for arithmetic in the cyclic polynomial ring (modulo `x^{N} - 1`).
L77: Prime field  | Custom: User-selected prime `p` < `2`^{`62`}. Built-in: `BabyBear` / `KoalaBear`.
L78: Precomputed roots  | `BabyBear` / `KoalaBear`: `*_primitive_root_S` (`10` ≤ `S` ≤ `24`).
L79: See cite17†Prime Field Constants for built-in prime values and compile-time root symbols.
L80: 
L81: Both Standard NTT and Staged NTT support `uint16_t`, `uint32_t`, and `uint64_t` as precisions for any prime modulus. The next two subsections tabulate supported transform-size limits for Standard NTT and Staged NTT.

L57: ## 0.6.0cite43†# L58: 
L59: This release includes the following updates:
L60: 
L61:   * New Libraries
L62: 
L63:     * cuPQC-BigInt (Multi-Precision Integer Arithmetic): a new device-side library for fixed-width unsigned multi-precision integer arithmetic, callable directly from CUDA kernels. Single-thread and warp-cooperative (`TPI`) execution for widths from 32 to 4096 bits, modular arithmetic and modular inverse, Barrett and Montgomery reduction, double-width products, and configurable error-handling policies.
L64:     * cuPQC-NTT (Number Theoretic Transform): a new device-side library for forward and inverse NTT, callable directly from CUDA kernels. Support for any custom prime field, transform lengths 2^{2} through 2^{24}, built-in BabyBear and KoalaBear primes with pre-computed primitive roots for 2^{10} through 2^{24}, and a staged two-pass mode (`SubSize<M>`) for transforms whose working set exceeds a single block’s shared memory.
L65: 
L66:   * Documentation
L67:     * The documentation now covers all four libraries, each with Features, Usage Guide, and API Reference sections.
L68: 
L69:   * Known Limitations
L70: 
L71:     * cuPQC-BigInt builds a specific set of bit widths for each `TPI`. A width outside that set compiles but fails to link; see cite44†Supported Widths .
L72: 
L73:     * Several cuPQC-BigInt operations are built for thread execution only, including division and remainder, the scalar conversions, and the trapping error policies; see cite45†Warp Execution Coverage .
